title: Where 4 percent came from
teaches: Bengen's rule and the Trinity study, run on every start since 1871, and what a success rate does and doesn't measure

blocks.text: In the early 1990s Bill Bengen, a financial planner in El Cajon, California, kept being asked the same thing by clients about to retire: how much can I take out each year without running out? The usual answer in the trade came from averages. Shares had returned about 10 percent a year since 1926 and inflation had run about 3, so a balanced portfolio should earn 7 percent or so, and a client could spend something near that.

Bengen distrusted it. An average return says nothing about the order the returns arrive in, and a retiree who meets a crash in year two is in a different position from one who meets it in year twenty-two. So he did something simple and laborious. He took the record of US large-company shares, intermediate government bonds and inflation from 1926, and for every possible starting year he played out a retirement: take a set percentage of the starting balance in the first year, raise that dollar amount by inflation every year after, and see whether the money lasted thirty years.

He published the result in the Journal of Financial Planning in October 1994. With half to three quarters of the money in shares, the highest starting rate that had survived every thirty-year period in the record was a little over 4 percent. The worst case was a retirement beginning in 1966. Seven percent, the figure the averages suggested, would have run out in well under twenty years for many starts.[^bengen]

blocks.text: The figure does what Bengen did, on a longer record: US shares, ten-year Treasury bonds and consumer prices from 1871 to 2022, a year at a time, January to January. Every line is one retirement that started in a different year, with a balance of one unit. The balance is drawn after inflation, so a line that stays level kept its buying power, and a line that reaches zero ran out. The strip underneath shows every start year, red for the ones that failed.
Make a guess first. Then move the withdrawal rate and the mix of shares and bonds, and watch which starting years turn red.

blocks.caption: Every 30-year retirement from 1871 to 1993, a balance of one unit, spending a fixed real amount each year. The dotted line is the starting balance.
blocks.task: Guess, then move the withdrawal and the share in stocks

blocks.text: At 4 percent with 60 percent in shares, five starts fail, and they are neighbours: 1965 to 1969. Every other start since 1871 lasted thirty years, and most ended with more than they began with, after inflation. Drop to 3.75 percent and only 1965 and 1966 fail. Rise to 5 percent and a quarter of all starts fail: most of the years from 1899 to 1916, 1929 and 1937, and nearly every start from 1956 to 1973.[^data]

Two things stand out. Failures cluster: a bad start is a bad era, not a bad year, and neighbouring retirements fail together because they share most of their returns. And the mix matters at the extremes. With all the money in bonds, even 3.5 percent fails a third of the time, because bonds barely beat inflation over long stretches. Somewhere between half and all of the money in shares, the results flatten out.

The crash of 1929 is the event everyone remembers, so it is surprising that a retiree of 1929 survived. Prices fell by about a quarter in the early 1930s, so a fixed real withdrawal was a shrinking dollar withdrawal, and bonds did well. The retiree's balance was battered but the spending it had to cover fell with prices.

The retiree of 1966 met the opposite. Shares went sideways for sixteen years: the S&P 500 stood near where it had started in 1982, while consumer prices nearly tripled. Bonds lost money after inflation through most of the 1970s, because their fixed coupons were overtaken by rising prices. The retiree raised withdrawals every year to keep up with prices while the portfolio's real value sank, and by the time shares recovered there was too little left for the recovery to rescue.

This is the first appearance of the course's most important idea. The 1966 retiree's thirty-year average return was not terrible. What ruined it was having the worst stretch first, while the balance was largest and withdrawals were the biggest share of it. Lesson 3 takes that apart.

In 1998 three finance professors at Trinity University in San Antonio, Philip Cooley, Carl Hubbard and Daniel Walz, published tables that made Bengen's method famous. For each withdrawal rate and each mix of shares and bonds they counted what share of historical periods had lasted. Their 4 percent, 50/50 cell read 95 percent, and "the 4 percent rule" entered popular finance.

blocks.caption: The same kind of table from this course's data: the share of 30-year starts from 1871 to 1993 in which a fixed real withdrawal lasted.

blocks.text: A success rate is easy to read and easy to misread. Three cautions:

**The starts are not independent.** There are 123 thirty-year starts between 1871 and 1993, but they overlap almost entirely, and there are only five separate thirty-year stretches in the whole record. A 95 percent success rate means "the plan failed in one bad era out of roughly five", not "a 1 in 20 chance".

**Failure and success hide the size.** A plan that ran out in year 29 counts as a failure; one that ended with a single dollar counts as a success. Meanwhile, at 4 percent the middle start ended with more than its starting balance after inflation, and many ended with two or three times as much. A retiree who knew which kind of era they were in would have spent very differently.

**Nobody actually behaves like this.** The rule assumes the retiree raises spending with inflation every year, whatever happens to the portfolio, and never adjusts. Real people cut back in bad years and loosen up in good ones. Lesson 5 shows how much a little flexibility is worth.

Read carefully, "the 4 percent rule" is a narrow historical claim: a starting withdrawal of 4 percent of the balance, raised with US inflation every year, from a portfolio of US shares and bonds with no fees, lasted thirty years from almost every start in the record. Each part of that sentence matters for what follows.
**Thirty years.** Bengen's clients were retiring at 65. Lesson 4 runs the same method over forty and fifty years.
**No fees.** A 1 percent advisory fee takes a quarter of a 4 percent withdrawal. Set the fee slider to 1 percent and seventeen starts fail where five did.
**Before tax.** The withdrawals are gross. Whether $40,000 out of a portfolio buys $40,000 of life or $33,000 depends on which accounts it comes from, which is part two of the course.

**One country's luck.** The US had one of the best stock markets of the twentieth century. Investors in Japan, Italy or Germany over the same years would have found a much lower safe rate. Lesson 6 looks at that.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Bengen's method: withdraw a set share of the starting balance, raise it with inflation, and test every historical start.
On this course's data, 4 percent from 60/40 fails only for retirements beginning in 1965 to 1969.
A success rate counts overlapping periods, says nothing about how much was left, and assumes no one ever adjusts.

blocks.caption: Six questions on the 4 percent rule
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Under Bengen's rule, a retiree with $1,000,000 takes $40,000 in the first year. Inflation that year is 5 percent and the portfolio falls 20 percent. What does the rule say to take in year two?
items.why: The rule keeps the real amount fixed: the first year's dollars, raised by inflation, whatever the portfolio did. $40,000 × 1.05 = $42,000.

items.ask: Why did a retirement starting in 1929 survive when one starting in 1966 did not?
choices: Prices fell in the early 1930s, shrinking the dollar withdrawals, while the 1970s brought high inflation and flat shares
The 1929 crash was smaller than the 1970s bear market
items.why: Deflation in the early 1930s cut the real cost of a fixed dollar amount and helped bonds. In the 1970s inflation raised the withdrawals while shares went sideways and bonds lost value after inflation.

items.ask: A table says a 4 percent withdrawal had a 95 percent success rate over 30 years. Which reading is closest to right?
choices: It failed in one bad historical era, among about five, which the overlapping starts share
There is a 1 in 20 chance of running out
It will last 30 years 95 percent of the time in future
items.why: The 123 starts overlap heavily, so the record holds only about five separate thirty-year periods. The failures come from one cluster of years, not independent draws.

items.ask: Why do success rates fall when the portfolio is all in bonds?
choices: Over long stretches bonds have barely beaten inflation, so they can't support a withdrawal raised with prices
Bonds are more volatile than shares
items.why: US bonds returned about 2 to 3 percent a year after inflation over the record, and lost value in real terms through the 1940s and 1970s. A 4 percent real withdrawal outruns them.

items.ask: At 4 percent from a 60/40 portfolio, how did the middle (median) start end after 30 years?
choices: With somewhat more than its starting balance, after inflation
items.why: Most starts did far better than the worst case. The median ended a little above where it began in real terms, and many ended with two or three times as much.

items.ask: What does a 1 percent yearly advisory fee do to a 4 percent withdrawal plan in this record?
choices: Failures rise from five starts to seventeen
items.why: A 1 percent fee is a quarter of a 4 percent withdrawal, taken every year whatever the market does. It pushes many marginal starts into failure.

summary: **Bengen tested history, not averages.** He played out a retirement from every starting year and found the highest starting withdrawal that always lasted 30 years.
**The rule is a starting rate raised with inflation.** Take 4 percent of the first balance, then the same real amount every year, whatever markets do.
**On this course's data, 4 percent from 60/40 fails only for 1965 to 1969 starts.** The worst start, 1966, supports about 3.6 percent.
**The worst era was the late 1960s, not 1929.** Rising prices and flat shares hurt more than a crash followed by deflation.
**Success rates count overlapping periods.** There are only about five separate thirty-year stretches since 1871.
**Most starts ended richer.** At 4 percent the median start finished above its starting balance after inflation.
**The rule leaves things out.** It assumes 30 years, no fees, no taxes, no flexibility and US history.

bengen.title: SAFEMAX
bengen.text: Bengen called the highest rate that survived every start the SAFEMAX, and the phrase "4 percent rule" came later, from others. His 1994 figure was about 4.15 percent, from 1966. In later papers he added small-company shares to the portfolio, which raised the figure to about 4.5 percent.

data.title: Why this course's 1966 figure is lower
data.text: Bengen used intermediate-term government bonds from 1926 and drew his figure from those years. This course uses Robert Shiller's series back to 1871 with ten-year Treasuries, takes each year's withdrawal at the start of the year and uses January-to-January years. Those choices put the 1966 start near 3.6 percent for 60/40 rather than 4.15. Different reasonable data sets move the worst case by a few tenths of a percent, which is itself worth knowing.
